choices.why: Sulfur sits below oxygen in the same column. The larger atom holds its electrons more loosely and is solvated less tightly, so it reaches carbon faster. This is the {{HS-}} (126,000) against {{HO-}} (16,000) comparison with a methyl group on each.
This ranks by basicity. Methoxide is the stronger base (methanol {{pKa}} 15.5 against about 10.5 for a thiol), but in a column the stronger base is the weaker nucleophile.

steps.h: The atom that carries the negative charge attacks: S in {{CH3S-}}, O in {{CH3O-}}. Both are anions and both carry one methyl group, so charge and bulk are the same.

ask.q: What is the only difference between the two species?
ask.a: The attacking atom: sulfur or oxygen.

steps.t: Place the atoms in the periodic table
steps.h: Oxygen and sulfur are in the same column, with sulfur one row lower.

ask.a: Same column. Sulfur is below oxygen.

steps.h: The lecture's sketch: basicity increases to the left and up, nucleophilicity increases to the left and down. In a column the two run in opposite directions. The larger atom is more polarizable, and a protic solvent holds the smaller ion more tightly.

ask.q: Which of the two is the stronger base?
ask.a: Methoxide. It is still the weaker nucleophile.

steps.h: The table has the parent pair: {{HS-}} 126,000 and {{HO-}} 16,000. A methyl group on each does not change the order.

solution.rule: Same column: the lower atom is the better nucleophile, although it is the weaker base.

choices.why: tert-Butoxide is the stronger base (tert-butanol {{pKa}} 17 against water 15.7), but three methyl groups surround the oxygen. The lecture calls it a poor nucleophile.
Same attacking atom and same charge, but nothing crowds the oxygen. Hydroxide gets to the back of the carbon easily: 16,000 in the lecture table.

steps.h: Oxygen in both, with a negative charge in both. The row and column trends compare different atoms, so they cannot decide this pair.

ask.q: Do the periodic trends help here?
ask.a: No. The attacking atom is the same.

steps.h: Hydroxide carries one hydrogen. tert-Butoxide carries a carbon with three methyl groups. The lecture's rule: a bulkier nucleophile is less nucleophilic.

ask.q: Why does bulk matter for attack on carbon?
ask.a: The nucleophile must come close to the back of a carbon that already has three groups on it. Bulk on both sides collides.

steps.h: Taking a proton is not hindered, because a hydrogen is small and exposed. So tert-butoxide stays a strong base while being a poor nucleophile.

ask.q: Which one is the stronger base?

steps.h: Same atom, same charge, less bulk: hydroxide is the stronger nucleophile.

solution.rule: Same atom and charge: the less hindered species is the better nucleophile.

choices.why: Nitrogen is to the left of oxygen in the same row: less electronegative, so its lone pair is more available. Lecture table: {{NH3}} 8,000.
Oxygen holds its lone pairs more tightly than nitrogen does. Lecture table: {{H2O}} 1, eight thousand times slower than ammonia.

steps.h: N in ammonia, O in water. Both molecules are neutral and both attack with a lone pair.

ask.q: Is charge different between the two?
ask.a: No. Both are neutral, so charge cannot decide.

steps.t: Place the atoms in the periodic table
steps.h: Nitrogen and oxygen are neighbours in the same row, with nitrogen to the left.
Across a row nucleophilicity follows basicity, and both increase to the left. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so it shares its lone pair more readily.

ask.q: Which is the stronger base, ammonia or water?
ask.a: Ammonia. In a row the stronger base is also the stronger nucleophile.

solution.rule: Same row: the atom further left is the better nucleophile (and the better base).

choices.why: The attacking atom is also a negative oxygen, but the charge is shared between two oxygens by resonance, so less of it is available. Lecture table: acetate 630.
The negative charge sits on one oxygen, fully available to attack. Ethoxide behaves like hydroxide (16,000 in the lecture table).

steps.h: A negatively charged oxygen in both. Same atom, same charge.

ask.q: Can the row or column trend decide?
ask.a: No. Both attack with a negative oxygen.

steps.h: Neither oxygen is crowded: each is attached to one carbon that is not heavily substituted. Bulk does not decide either.
Draw the second resonance form of acetate: the charge moves to the other oxygen. Each oxygen carries only half of the charge. In ethoxide there is no second form.

ask.q: Where is the negative charge in acetate?
ask.a: Shared equally by the two oxygens.

steps.h: A delocalized charge makes a weaker base (acetic acid {{pKa}} 4 against ethanol 15.9) and, for the same attacking atom, a weaker nucleophile. The lecture table shows it: {{CH3CO2-}} 630, {{HO-}} 16,000.

ask.q: Which lecture value stands in for ethoxide?
ask.a: Hydroxide, 16,000: a negative oxygen with a localized charge.

solution.rule: Same atom and charge: a charge delocalized by resonance is less nucleophilic.

choices.why: Bromine is below chlorine in the same column: larger, more polarizable, less tightly solvated.
This ranks by basicity. Chloride is the stronger base (HCl {{pKa}} -8 against HBr -9) but the weaker nucleophile.

steps.h: Br and Cl. Both are anions with no groups attached.
Same column (the halogens). Bromine is one row lower.
Nucleophilicity increases down a column: {{I-}} > {{Br-}} > {{Cl-}}. The lecture table gives the two ends, 80,000 and 1,000, and bromide falls between them.

solution.rule: Down a column: bigger atom, better nucleophile.

choices.why: Water attacks with the same atom but has no negative charge to push its electrons toward carbon. Lecture table: {{H2O}} 1.
The anion has more electron density to give than its own conjugate acid. Lecture table: {{HO-}} 16,000.

steps.h: Oxygen in both.
Hydroxide is water with one proton removed. It is negatively charged, water is neutral.
With the same attacking atom, the anion is the better nucleophile. Lecture table: 16,000 against 1.

solution.rule: An anion is a better nucleophile than its neutral conjugate acid.

choices.why: Amide ion is ammonia with a proton removed: same nitrogen, now with a negative charge. It is the better nucleophile and also a very strong base (ammonia {{pKa}} 38).
Ammonia is a good neutral nucleophile (8,000), but its own conjugate base beats it.

steps.h: Nitrogen in both.
{{NH2-}} is the conjugate base of {{NH3}}: one is an anion, the other neutral.
Same atom: the anion wins, exactly as {{HO-}} (16,000) beats {{H2O}} (1).

solution.rule: Same atom: the species with the negative charge is the better nucleophile.

choices.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and holds its electrons tightly. Fluoride is a weak base (HF {{pKa}} 4) and a poor nucleophile.
Oxygen is to the left of fluorine in the same row. It is less electronegative, so hydroxide is both the stronger base and the stronger nucleophile.

steps.h: O and F, both carrying a negative charge.
Same row, oxygen to the left of fluorine.
Across a row nucleophilicity follows basicity and increases to the left. Water ({{pKa}} 15.7) is a much weaker acid than HF (4), so hydroxide is the stronger base and the stronger nucleophile.

solution.rule: Same row: nucleophilicity follows basicity, increasing to the left.

choices.why: Iodide is at the bottom of the column: the largest and most polarizable halide, 80,000 in the lecture table.
Fluoride is the strongest base of the halides, but it is small, holds its electrons tightly and is strongly solvated. It is the poorest nucleophile of the four.

steps.h: I and F, both anions.
Same column, at opposite ends: fluorine at the top, iodine at the bottom.
Nucleophilicity increases down the column while basicity decreases. HF has {{pKa}} 4 and HI -10: fluoride is by far the stronger base and still the weaker nucleophile.

solution.rule: Down a column the trends split: weaker base, better nucleophile.

choices.why: Acetic acid is neutral. Its oxygens hold their lone pairs tightly, and it would rather give up a proton than attack carbon.
Acetate carries a negative charge. Even shared between two oxygens, it makes acetate a much better nucleophile than its neutral acid (630 in the lecture table).

steps.h: Oxygen in both.
Acetate is the conjugate base of acetic acid: an anion against a neutral molecule.
Same atom: the anion is the better nucleophile. Acetate is modest among anions (630) but far ahead of neutral oxygen nucleophiles such as {{CH3OH}} and {{H2O}} (1).

solution.rule: An anion is a better nucleophile than its neutral conjugate acid.

choices.why: Nitrogen is to the left of oxygen in the same row: less electronegative, so the lone pairs are more available. Amide is the stronger base and the stronger nucleophile.
Hydroxide is a good nucleophile (16,000), but oxygen holds its electrons more tightly than nitrogen.

steps.h: N and O, each with a negative charge and only hydrogens attached.
Same row, nitrogen to the left.
Nucleophilicity and basicity both increase to the left in a row. Ammonia ({{pKa}} 38) is a far weaker acid than water (15.7), so {{NH2-}} is the stronger base and the stronger nucleophile.

solution.rule: Same row: further left means more basic and more nucleophilic.

choices.why: Chlorine is more electronegative than sulfur and holds its charge more tightly. Lecture table: 1,000.
Sulfur is to the left of chlorine in the same row, so {{HS-}} is the stronger base and the stronger nucleophile. Lecture table: 126,000.

steps.h: S and Cl, both anions.
Same row (the third), sulfur to the left of chlorine.

steps.t: Use the row trend and check
steps.h: To the left means more nucleophilic. The lecture table agrees: {{HS-}} 126,000 against {{Cl-}} 1,000.

solution.rule: The row trend works in every row: further left, better nucleophile.

choices.why: Same negative oxygen, but with only a primary carbon attached it can reach the electrophile.
This is the stronger base (tert-butanol {{pKa}} 17 against ethanol 15.9), which is the tempting reason to circle it. Its bulk makes it the poorer nucleophile.

steps.h: A negative oxygen in both. The periodic trends do not apply.
Ethoxide has a {{CH2CH3}} group on oxygen. tert-Butoxide has a carbon with three methyl groups.
Bulkier nucleophile, less nucleophilic. tert-Butoxide is the lecture's example of a strong base that is a poor nucleophile.

solution.rule: Same atom and charge: less bulk, better nucleophile.

choices.why: The charge is shared by two oxygens through resonance, so each oxygen is less able to attack. Lecture table: 630.
The charge is on one oxygen and fully available. Lecture table: 16,000.

steps.h: A negative oxygen in both.
Acetate has two equivalent resonance forms. Hydroxide has one structure only.
{{HO-}} 16,000, {{CH3CO2-}} 630: about 25 times slower. The same resonance makes acetic acid ({{pKa}} 4) far more acidic than water (15.7).

solution.rule: Resonance spreads the charge out and lowers nucleophilicity.

choices.why: Sulfur is below oxygen. The column trend holds for neutral molecules as well as for anions: the larger atom gives up its lone pair more easily.
Water is one of the weakest nucleophiles in the lecture table (1). Oxygen is small and holds its lone pairs tightly.

steps.h: S and O. Both molecules are neutral, so charge does not decide.
Same column, sulfur lower.
Nucleophilicity increases down a column. The anions show it in the lecture table ({{HS-}} 126,000, {{HO-}} 16,000), and the neutral molecules follow the same order.

solution.rule: The column trend does not need a charge: lower atom, better nucleophile.

choices.why: The attacking atom is oxygen. Lecture table: {{CH3OH}} 1.
The attacking atom is nitrogen, to the left of oxygen in the same row. An amine behaves like ammonia (8,000).

steps.h: The lone pair on N in methylamine, on O in methanol. The carbon does not attack.
Both neutral, both carrying one methyl group. Only the atom differs.
Nitrogen is to the left of oxygen: more basic and more nucleophilic. The lecture table gives the parent pair, {{NH3}} 8,000 against {{H2O}} or {{CH3OH}} 1.

solution.rule: Neutral nucleophiles follow the same row trend: N beats O.

choices.why: Iodide is a very weak base but an excellent nucleophile: large and polarizable. Lecture table: 80,000.
Hydroxide is much the stronger base, which makes it tempting. Nucleophilicity is a measured rate, and the lecture table puts hydroxide at 16,000, five times slower than iodide.

steps.h: I and O. They are in different rows and different columns, so no single trend settles it.
HI has {{pKa}} -10 and water 15.7. Hydroxide is the stronger base by a huge margin, but basicity is an equilibrium and nucleophilicity is a rate.

solution.rule: When the atoms share neither row nor column, use the memorized table, not basicity.

choices.why: A good nucleophile, 16,000, but about eight times slower than acetylide.
Carbon is to the left of oxygen in the same row. The acetylide ion is a carbanion, a stronger base than hydroxide and a better nucleophile. Lecture table: 126,000.

steps.h: The negatively charged carbon of {{HC≡C-}} and the oxygen of {{HO-}}.
C and O are in the same row, carbon further left.

steps.t: Use the row trend and check
steps.h: Further left means more basic and more nucleophilic. An alkyne C-H has {{pKa}} 25 against 15.7 for water, and the lecture table gives {{HC≡C-}} 126,000 against {{HO-}} 16,000.

solution.rule: Same row: a carbanion is a better nucleophile than an oxygen anion.

choices.why: Azide attacks through nitrogen and is a good nucleophile. Lecture table: 8,000.
Acetate attacks through oxygen, and its charge is delocalized over two oxygens. Lecture table: 630.

steps.h: An end nitrogen of azide, an oxygen of acetate. Both species are anions.
N is to the left of O in the same row, which favours azide.

solution.rule: Nitrogen nucleophiles beat oxygen nucleophiles of the same row; acetate is weakened further by resonance.

choices.why: Azide is a good nucleophile, but its charge is spread over the two end nitrogens by resonance. Lecture table: 8,000, half the rate of hydroxide.
A full negative charge on one small oxygen. Lecture table: 16,000.

steps.h: O in hydroxide, an end N in azide.
The row trend favours nitrogen, but azide is delocalized by resonance while hydroxide has a localized charge. Rules that pull in opposite directions cannot give the answer.

solution.rule: When two rules disagree, the memorized table decides.

choices.why: The charge stays on the oxygen. An ordinary alkoxide, a strong base (ethanol {{pKa}} 15.9) and a good nucleophile.

The attacking atom is the same negative oxygen, but its charge is delocalized into the ring by resonance. That is why phenol ({{pKa}} 10) is more acidic than an alcohol, and it makes phenoxide the weaker nucleophile.

steps.h: A negative oxygen in both. The trends for different atoms do not apply.
In phenoxide the charge can be drawn on three ring carbons as well as on oxygen. In ethoxide it has nowhere to go.
Same atom, same charge: the species with the delocalized charge is the weaker base and the weaker nucleophile. It is the acetate (630) against hydroxide (16,000) pattern.

solution.rule: Same atom: delocalizing the charge lowers both basicity and nucleophilicity.

choices.why: The trap is to circle the one with the negative charge. The charge rule compares the same atom only. Chloride is small, electronegative and well solvated: 1,000 in the lecture table.
Ammonia is neutral, yet its nitrogen lone pair is so available that the lecture table gives it 8,000.

steps.h: N (neutral) and Cl (anion). Different atoms, different rows, different columns.
The charge rule compares a species with its own conjugate acid, so it does not apply. The row and column trends do not apply either.
{{NH3}} 8,000, {{Cl-}} 1,000. A neutral nitrogen beats a chloride anion.

solution.rule: A negative charge only wins when the attacking atom is the same.

choices.why: Chloride is a modest nucleophile, 1,000 in the lecture table, but it is ahead of acetate.
Acetate is by far the stronger base (acetic acid {{pKa}} 4 against HCl -8), which makes it tempting. Its charge is delocalized over two oxygens, and the lecture table gives it 630.

steps.h: Cl and O. Both anions, in different rows and columns.
Acetate is the stronger base by twelve {{pKa}} units. That does not make it the faster nucleophile.

solution.rule: Acetate is near the bottom of the anions in the table: resonance costs it nucleophilicity.

choices.why: Iodide is an excellent nucleophile, 80,000, and it is the larger atom, so it is easy to pick. It is still behind {{HS-}}.
{{HS-}} is at the top of the lecture table with 126,000.

steps.h: S and I. Both are large, polarizable atoms, and both are anions.
They share neither a row nor a column, so the trends alone do not rank them. Sulfur is further left, iodine is further down.

solution.rule: Know the top of the table: {{HC≡C-}} and {{HS-}} 126,000, then {{I-}} 80,000, then {{HO-}} 16,000.

choices.why: A negative nitrogen with only two hydrogens on it: nothing blocks its approach to carbon.
Diisopropylamide has the same negative nitrogen, but two isopropyl groups surround it. Like tert-butoxide, it is a strong base and a poor nucleophile.

steps.h: A negative nitrogen in both.
Two hydrogens on nitrogen in {{NH2-}}; two branched isopropyl groups in diisopropylamide.
Bulkier nucleophile, less nucleophilic. The rule was shown for oxygen (tert-butoxide) and works the same way for nitrogen.

solution.rule: Bulk around the attacking atom lowers nucleophilicity, whatever the atom.

choices.why: This ranks by basicity. The amine is the stronger base, but in a column the lower atom is the better nucleophile.
Phosphorus is below nitrogen in the same column. Its lone pair is held more loosely, so the phosphine attacks carbon faster even though it is the weaker base.

steps.h: The lone pair on P in trimethylphosphine and on N in trimethylamine. Both neutral, both with three methyl groups.
N and P are in the same column, phosphorus one row lower.
Nucleophilicity increases down a column, as it does from O to S and from Cl to I. The same reasoning applies to N and P.

solution.rule: The column trend applies to every column: P beats N, S beats O, I beats Cl.

choices.why: Neutral, but a nitrogen lone pair is a good nucleophile: 8,000 in the lecture table.
Acetate has the negative charge, which is the tempting reason to circle it. Its charge is delocalized over two oxygens: 630 in the lecture table.

steps.h: N (neutral) in ammonia, O (anion) in acetate.
The charge rule compares the same atom, so it does not settle this. The row trend (N left of O) favours ammonia, and resonance weakens acetate.

solution.rule: Do not circle a species only because it is charged: check the atom and check for resonance.

choices.why: Tosylate also has a negative oxygen, but the charge is shared by three oxygens. That stability is what makes it a good leaving group, and a good leaving group is a poor nucleophile.
The charge is on one oxygen, and the group attached is small. A strong base and a good nucleophile.

steps.h: A negative oxygen in both.
In tosylate, {{TsO-}}, the charge is delocalized over the three oxygens on sulfur. In methoxide it is localized.

steps.t: Connect to what you know about tosylate
steps.h: The lecture calls tosylate a good leaving group: a very weak, stable base. The same stability means it has little drive to attack carbon. Methoxide, the conjugate base of methanol ({{pKa}} 15.5), is far more reactive.

solution.rule: Good leaving groups are stable, weak bases, so they are poor nucleophiles.
